what: Equal-link knee press with passive spring-loaded platen. A bounded equal-link knee press. Motor A turns the first 32 mm link; an equal second link joins it to a passive platen held by real linear guides. The platen compresses one complete stock 9L shock absorber. The two-link mechanism moves in a horizontal plane, from a saved input angle of 40° to 15° and back. Only the input link is driven; the platen and shock move through the physical joints. It is a near-toggle pressing demonstration within the slider-crank family, not a bistable latch. One motor straightens two equal links against a stock shock load. The passive platen advances less per degree near alignment while the ideal output force per input torque rises. The finite program stops short of dead centre and returns.
try: Load the saved Final Squeeze model and its matching program, then use Robot Lab’s Run button. Reload the saved model before repeating, after interruption or after manual movement. The program starts at 40°, visits five further pressing angles in 5° steps down to 15°, then retraces those five steps. Speed commands are capped at ±8 degrees per second and decrease with the measured angle error near each target. The program captures hold when the reported error is below 0.15°, allows at most two recaptures and checks each settled arrival from fresh motor-angle readings.

Watch both equal links, the guided platen and the shock separately. Compare the platen advance in the first 5° pressing step with the final 5° step. Predict which step should advance farther, then use the independent output markers rather than treating encoder arrival as proof of platen motion.

At the 15° hold, compare the actual shock compression with its saved preload. Read the packaged native measurements and the independent geometric prediction. The ideal total platen travel is 12.792 mm; any measured difference belongs to the declared simulator and observation scope.

Observe the return through the same angles and the final return to the saved pose. Compare matching outward and return stages. The software completed flag reports the end of finite input commands; use the native observer evidence to assess the passive output and spring. Keep the supplied finite route; zero degrees and over-centre motion are outside it.
why: As the two equal links straighten, a given angular change produces a smaller change in their total horizontal projection. On the selected branch the platen coordinate is twice the link length times the cosine of the input angle. In an ideal slow, lossless mechanism, input work equals output work. Less output travel for the same input rotation therefore means more output force per unit of input torque. This does not mean a fixed-torque experiment was performed: the program controls input angle and the spring load changes throughout the route.
matters: A knee press combines a larger approach movement with a finer final squeeze. The geometry is useful when a mechanism needs low travel and a high ideal load ratio near the end of its stroke. Final Squeeze makes this visible with a real passive slider and a nominal spring load. Rod Ratio instead compares complete slider-crank strokes with unequal connecting rods; Snapgate crosses a spring-force line to store either of two states; Equal Share divides a load between separate spring branches.
question: If the input moves through equal 5° steps, should the platen advance equally? At 15° does the larger ideal force per input torque prove that the motor torque or actual force became that many times larger?
answer: No. The platen advances progressively less as the links approach alignment. The ideal local force-per-input-torque ratio is 2.484 times its value at 40° when the input reaches 15°. This compares transmission geometry at two angles, not measured motor torque or an actual force multiplication experiment. The shock force depends on its compression and assumed spring law. The finite route never reaches the dead-centre singularity.
further: Use x = 2L cos θ to predict every held platen coordinate and subtract successive values. Compare predictions made before the run with independent native body markers at actual measured input angles. A motor target alone cannot prove geometric closure.

Differentiate x with respect to θ in radians, then apply τ dθ = F dx. Keep units explicit: F/τ has units of inverse metres. If a different transmission were added, distinguish input-link torque from motor-shaft torque and include its ratio and losses.

The native spring force inferred as kδ uses the simulator’s nominal stiffness. Measure δ along the cylinder bore, not as an arbitrary diagonal between mounting eyes. Damping and constraint reactions are separate from the elastic term; real spring calibration, friction, strength and motor limits remain untested.

The source model uses two CAD components for one intact factory-sprung 9L shock. The platen stays passive and physically guided; there is no scripted output coordinate. This finite pressing/release experiment does not demonstrate unpowered latching, over-centre stability, infinite force or hardware capacity.
formula: Equal pivot spans L = 32 mm, positive selected branch: x(θ) = 2L cos θ; advance from home s = 2L(cos θ − cos θ_home). For θ in radians, |dx/dθ| = 2L sin θ. Ideal quasistatic virtual work at the input-link axis gives F/|τ| = 1/(2L sin θ), with L in metres for N per N·m. This dimensional ratio is not a dimensionless force multiplier. The supplied motor drives this input axis directly; no transmission ratio is assumed. With the actual shock axis parallel to platen travel, axial compression is inferred from the observed cylinder/rod separation and the source rest length; F_spring = kδ is a source-law prediction. No actuator torque, frictional efficiency, physical load rating or infinite force is established by these formulas.
